# Sickle Cell Disease: The Most African Disease, Under-Represented in Its Own Trial Base

---

## Abstract

**Background:** Sickle cell disease (SCD) is the world's most common severe
monogenic disorder — ~300,000 births/year, ~75% in sub-Saharan Africa [2] — yet
its evidence base was built almost entirely in high-income populations.

**Methods:** Full-registry AACT April-12-2026 analysis. A trial was counted as
"African-site" if ≥1 facility country was among the 54 African Union states.
For SCD and comparator conditions we computed global trial count, African-site
count, and within-disease African share, all as exact registry counts.

**Results:** 1,091 global SCD trials; 105 (9.62%) include an African site (788
interventional; 89 African = 11.29%). SCD's African share (9.6%) is roughly
double the 4.33% registry baseline — reflecting the disease's African burden —
yet **90% of trials for the most African-burdened disease still have no African
site.** Across comparators the African share was: HIV 18.8% (1,713/9,126),
zoonotic diseases 22.9% (99/432), cervical/HPV 5.2% (136/2,613), epilepsy 3.4%
(72/2,103), breast cancer 2.6% (375/14,432). SCD's global trial base (1,091) is
one-eighth the size of breast cancer's (14,432) despite comparable or greater
contribution to early-childhood mortality in endemic regions.

**Conclusion:** SCD sits in a paradox: above-baseline African representation on a
proportional basis, but a small absolute trial base and near-total absence of
African sites for a disease three-quarters African by birth. The gap is a
funding-and-priority decision — the REACH trial [7] proved African SCD trials
are feasible — not a logistical impossibility.

---

## 1. Introduction

SCD arises from a single β-globin variant (HBB codon 6, Glu→Val) producing
haemoglobin S; homozygosity (HbSS) drives vaso-occlusion, haemolytic anaemia,
and infection susceptibility. The HbS allele reached high frequency in
malaria-endemic regions through heterozygote advantage (HbAS confers partial
protection against severe malaria), tying SCD geography to the historical
malaria belt [1]. Of ~300,000 annual SCD births, ~75% occur in sub-Saharan
Africa [2].

The therapeutic evidence base, by contrast, is HIC-derived. Hydroxyurea was
approved on the US Multicenter Study of Hydroxyurea (MSH) [3]; BABY HUG (young
children) was conducted entirely in the US [4]; voxelotor and crizanlizumab were
approved on largely North American/European trials; and curative CRISPR/lentiviral
gene therapies (approved 2023) were developed in HIC settings at ~$2–3 million
per course, building on early trials such as CTX001 [5]. The result is an
evidence base — and a treatment armamentarium — matched to the 25% of the birth
burden that is non-African.

---

## 2. Methods

**Data.** AACT April-12-2026 flat-file snapshot. Records reassembled by start
signature before field splitting (AACT text fields embed newlines).

**African-site trial.** ≥1 `facilities.country` among the 54 AU member states
(plus Western Sahara and African island territories). Registry-wide, 25,125
trials (4.33%) meet this; among interventional studies, 4.50%.

**Condition match.** `conditions.downcase_name` containing "sickle cell",
"sickle-cell", or "drepanocyt-"; comparators by analogous disease-specific
keyword sets (HIV, cervical/HPV, breast cancer, epilepsy, an aggregate
zoonotic set). Counts are distinct nct_ids. Aggregate categories (zoonotic; an
antimicrobial-resistance keyword set that returns only 259 trials and clearly
under-captures resistant-organism trials coded by specific pathogen) are flagged
as lower-precision and not used for headline claims.

**Metric.** Within-disease African share = African-site trials ÷ global trials
for that condition, compared to the 4.33% registry baseline.

---

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Cross-disease African-site trial share (AACT 2026-04-12)

| Condition | Global trials | African-site | African share | (interventional) African share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sickle cell disease** | 1,091 | 105 | **9.62%** | 11.29% |
| HIV / AIDS | 9,126 | 1,713 | 18.77% | 19.54% |
| Zoonotic (aggregate)* | 432 | 99 | 22.92% | 20.06% |
| Cervical cancer / HPV | 2,613 | 136 | 5.20% | 5.31% |
| Epilepsy | 2,103 | 72 | 3.42% | 3.68% |
| Breast cancer | 14,432 | 375 | 2.60% | 2.64% |
| **Registry baseline (all)** | 579,828 | 25,125 | **4.33%** | 4.50% |

\*Keyword-aggregated; lower precision, shown for context only.

Two facts stand out. **(1)** On a proportional basis SCD's African share (9.6%)
is roughly twice the registry baseline — the burden concentration does register
in the data. **(2)** But the absolute base is tiny: 1,091 global SCD trials
versus 14,432 for breast cancer, and only 105 of the SCD trials touch an African
site. For the disease whose burden is ~75% African, ~90% of its trials have no
African site.

### 3.2 Reconciliation with v1

v1 reported 102 SCD African-site trials within 24,771 African-site trials
(0.4%). v2 finds 105 SCD African-site trials within 25,125 (the small deltas are
snapshot timing plus the added "drepanocyt-" synonym). Both agree on the
substantive point; v2's within-disease denominator (9.6% of SCD trials) is the
more defensible headline than v1's share-of-portfolio (0.4%), which is dominated
by the rarity of African sites generally.

### 3.3 Treatment access context (from published trials, not registry)

- **Hydroxyurea** (generic, off-patent) is proven effective in African children
  by the REACH trial (Angola, DRC, Kenya, Uganda) [7], yet remains inaccessible
  in most African countries due to regulatory approval, prescribing-authority,
  and supply-chain barriers rather than drug cost.
- **Gene therapy** (approved 2023) creates an "access cliff": the first curative
  option is priced at ~$2–3 million/course, with no realistic African pathway on
  current funding models [5].
- **Newborn screening** — the gateway to prophylactic penicillin and early
  hydroxyurea — reaches only a handful of African countries in pilot form;
  precise country coverage is not derivable from the registry and is flagged for
  author verification against current in-country data.

---

## 4. Discussion

The SCD portfolio embodies an evidence-and-access double gap. On evidence: the
pharmacokinetics, optimal dosing, response rate, and complication profile of
hydroxyurea and newer agents in African populations — where malaria co-infection,
G6PD deficiency, and nutritional variation differ systematically from HIC trial
populations — remain under-characterised because ~90% of SCD trials have no
African site. On access: proven, cheap hydroxyurea is unavailable where it is
most needed, and curative therapy is priced beyond any African health system.

Crucially, the gap is not logistical. REACH [7] enrolled children in four
sub-Saharan countries without prior SCD-trial experience and demonstrated that
hydroxyurea reduces the rate of clinical events (vaso-occlusion, infections
including malaria, transfusion, and death) in African children — landmark
evidence generated on African soil with NIH/NHLBI and Burroughs Wellcome
support. The lesson is that the absence of African SCD trials reflects funding
and priority, not feasibility.

The most tractable near-term agenda is therefore not gene-therapy access but
hydroxyurea scale-up: national regulatory approval across African countries,
task-shifted prescribing, generic procurement, and newborn-screening expansion —
each technically feasible and each currently under-funded. In parallel, a
pan-African SCD trial network would convert the one-off REACH proof into standing
capacity, and give African patients a route into the next generation of
HbF-inducing and curative therapies.

The proportional-vs-absolute distinction matters for framing. It would be
inaccurate to say SCD is *proportionally* neglected relative to the average
disease — its 9.6% African share exceeds baseline. The accurate claim is
sharper: even the most African-burdened monogenic disease commands a small
absolute trial base, and even within that base African sites are the exception,
so the populations bearing three-quarters of the burden remain largely absent
from the evidence that governs their care.

---

## 5. Limitations

Registry counts undercount trials registered only on PACTR, ISRCTN, PACTR, or
national African registries not mirrored in ClinicalTrials.gov. Condition
keyword matching may miss trials where SCD is a secondary condition. DALY-per-
trial ratios require Africa-specific GBD 2019/2022 SCD estimates from the GBD
results tool and are not computed here [9]. Hydroxyurea country-level regulatory
status and newborn-screening coverage require author verification with current
in-country data. Registry-visible site absence does not by itself establish an
evidence deficiency for every clinical question, but the systematic pattern
across the therapeutic class is well documented.

---

## 6. Conclusion

Of 1,091 global sickle-cell-disease trials, 105 (9.6%) include an African site —
above the 4.33% registry baseline, but leaving ~90% of trials for the most
African-burdened disease without any African site, on a global base one-eighth
the size of breast cancer's. Proven hydroxyurea is unavailable across most of
Africa for tractable regulatory and supply reasons; curative gene therapy is
priced beyond reach. The REACH trial proves African SCD trials are feasible; the
gap is a matter of funding and priority. The remedy is a hydroxyurea-access
programme at the scale of the antiretroviral movement, universal newborn
screening, and a standing pan-African SCD trial network.
